stops.note: the edible innards of a deer; the l changed to n
'numbles' became 'umbles' by losing its n to the article; Samuel Pepys records on 8 July 1663 that Mrs Turner brought him an 'umble-pie hot out of her oven'
'humble pie' appears in print by 1669, and the pun later gave 'to eat humble pie', to be forced to apologise

current_meaning: (eat humble pie) to make a humble apology after being proved wrong
